title: Request preproc sampler + scheduler jitter notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working scratchpad collecting observations and quick hypotheses from recent sampling runs focused on how the request pre-processing pipeline (header parse, JSON deserialization, simple validation, and tokenization pre-pass) interacts with the OS scheduler and our Python worker threads. Pattern: low-payload (<350B) requests show spiky CPU profiles and sporadic tail latency (p95/p99 jitter) that correlate with sampler snapshots showing repeated short lived stacks stuck in Python C-extension boundaries and frequent syscalls (epoll_wait wakeups).

Why this matters:
- For small requests we are CPU-bound in preproc, so inefficiencies here amplify token-per-second cost and tail percentiles for real-time apps.
- Tail jitter is user-visible even when median is fine; it spikes throughput headroom estimations and makes autoscaler decisions noisy.

High-level observations from sampling runs (2026-01 to 2026-02):
- Workload: synthetic small-chat trace (avg payload 220 bytes, median tokens output ~16).
- p50 end-to-end: ~18 ms; p95: 46–120 ms (variable across runs); p99: up to 360 ms during cold scheduler states.
- CPU breakdown (micro-sampler + perf): ~60–75% of CPU time in python-layer preproc (header parse + JSON + small tokenization pre-pass), ~20% in kernel syscalls (epoll, futex), ~5–10% in model runtime startup and NV stuff (negligible for this tracer).
- Frequent frames in samples: orjson.dumps/loads (C extension), PyUnicode_Normalize (unicode normalizer), regex fast_search in tokenizer, signal handling trampolines, and PyThread_acquire_lock paths.

Representative flamegraph notes: (from run 2026-01-18)
- Dominant stack collapse: accept_conn -> parse_headers -> orjson.loads -> json_scan_object (C) -> back into Python for per-header checks -> unicode_normalize -> tokenizer.regex_scan.
- The transitions between C-extensions into Python (callbacks) show non-trivial overhead in samples.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Scheduler jitter + short-lived threads: We create many short-lived worker tasks to handle preproc for small requests; the kernel scheduler may be preempting these frequently and the overhead of park/unpark (or futex wait/wake) is visible in syscalls. Moving to a long-lived worker thread pool with task queues will reduce futex churn.
2) Crossing from orjson (C) back to Python to run small validation callbacks is expensive at scale: The C->Py boundary and GIL handoff cost is larger than the pure C parse for short inputs. We should batch validations or push them into C/Rust to stay in native land.
3) Unicode normalization and regex-driven token boundary scanning are disproportionate for ASCII-heavy short inputs. A fast-path byte-level scan when ASCII-only could knock down 20–40% of preproc cost.
4) Epoll wakeup patterns: using edge-triggered epoll with naive loop can cause extra wake cycles; moving to a combined level-triggered read buffer strategy reduces wakeups.

Experiments run so far (and quick results):
A) Long-lived worker pool (e.g., concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor with max_workers pinned to cpu_count() + 2): reduced futex syscalls by ~40% and p95 improved by ~10–15% for the synthetic run. However, p99 still exhibited rare spikes (requests co-scheduled with GC).
B) orjson -> fallback to pure Python for small objects: moving small-header validation into C (experimentally implemented as a tiny C helper) removed the C->Py callback for header checks and reduced per-request CPU by ~0.8ms (on median); p95 improved modestly.
C) ASCII fast-path tokenizer: implemented a simple C-accelerated fast path that returns early for ascii-only inputs; median preproc reduced by ~1.2ms and p95 improved by ~8ms on small payloads. This is promising but needs extensive correctness testing (unicode, combining chars).
D) Epoll mode swap (edge -> level + buffered reads): reduced epoll syscall rate by ~30% and reduced jitter in microbench, but introduced minor latency regression for very large payloads (rare for targeted workload).

Open evidence gaps / questions:
- Are we seeing GC pauses (young-gen) causing the p99 spikes? Sampler stacks sometimes show traces in gc.collect and PyObject_Malloc slow paths. Need runs with gc.disabled and tracemalloc to confirm.
- How much of the C->Py cost is due to GIL contention between parse threads and the main event loop thread? We should try the sub-interpreter experiment (pyisol/PEP 554) for isolating preproc threads.
- Are signal handlers (libc trampoline) waking threads for timers (our latency SLO timers) causing unnecessary interruptions? Samples occasionally show signal trampoline frames.

Actionable next experiments (short list):
1) Run a controlled A/B: baseline vs. long-lived pinned worker pool with gc thresholds tuned. Capture full perf + heap profiles and compare p99 events. Target metric: reduce p99 by >= 30% without regressing p50.
2) Implement minimal header-check C extension that returns a bitmask of failed checks (no callbacks). Measure the delta on the small-request workload.
3) Add an ASCII-detect fast-path in tokenizer: short-circuit normalization+regex when detection passes. Must include exhaustive tests for UTF-8 edge cases.
4) Re-run with Python sub-interpreters for preproc tasks to test whether GIL-crossing is the dominant issue (compare CPU and futex syscall counts).
5) Trace syscalls annotated with thread id across runs to identify which threads are causing futex wake/wait pairs.

Implementation considerations and risk notes:
- C extensions reduce runtime safety surface (memory bugs) and complicate packaging for Private deployments. Consider using a minimal Rust extension via PyO3 (safer memory model) and keep public API narrow.
- Sub-interpreters can help isolate GIL contention but break C extension state that relies on process-global objects; need audit of all extensions used in preproc.
- Fast-path heuristics must be conservative: false positives (skipping normalization when needed) could produce tokenization mismatches, affecting model outputs. Plan for canary flag and token-level diffs against golden set.

Quick checklist before merging a change: (for any optimization we ship)
- [ ] Unit tests for behavior parity vs. golden parser across ASCII/UTF-8 edgecases.
- [ ] Load test with synthetic small-request trace for 30 minutes, measure p50/p95/p99 and futex syscall rate.
- [ ] Canary on Dedicated region for a single customer with low-risk traffic, monitor telemetry for tokenization mismatch alerts and latency regressions.
- [ ] Security review for any C/Rust native code.

Notes for follow-up profiling scripts and experiments (command snippets):
- Lightweight sampler: run every 5 ms for 10s windows during a steady-state load (python -m pyflame or using linux perf record -F 99 --call-graph dwarf -p <pid> -- sleep 10).
- Syscall tracing: sudo perf trace -p <pid> -- sleep 10 or strace -f -c -p <pid> for counts.
- Threaded futex pairs: sudo perf script + custom parser to count futex_wait/futex_wake pairs grouped by tid.
- Small requester: wrk2 style client with header-heavy small payloads, ~800 rps per core equivalent.

Decision log:
- 2026-01-21: prioritize worker-pool experiment (done) -> partial wins, more investigation required.
- 2026-02-05: greenlight ASCII fast-path PoC (done) -> promising; escalate to correctness tests.

Outstanding decisions for engineering leads:
- Do we accept a small C/Rust dependency in serving runtime for the tokenization fast-path? (tradeoff: ~10–15% CPU for small-request workload vs packaging & security complexity).
- Do we pursue sub-interpreters as the long-term model for preproc isolation, or prefer to keep one process and tune GC/batching?

Appendix: quick microbench numbers (median ± std, sample from 2026-02-02)
- Baseline preproc (header+json+norm+tokenize): 3.9ms ± 0.5ms
- With long-lived pool: 3.1ms ± 0.4ms
- With C-header-check helper: 3.0ms ± 0.35ms
- With ASCII fast-path: 2.0ms ± 0.25ms (for ascii-only payloads)

Next steps (owners):
- Asha: run GC-disabled AB test and collect perf traces (due 2026-02-22)
